notes.meaning: The whole community of Israel gathered at Shiloh to set up the Tent of Meeting, which was the tabernacle for worshiping God. Shiloh was chosen under God's direction because the main fighting had ended and the area was secure. The tabernacle would remain at Shiloh for over three hundred years as the nation's center for worship and fellowship with God.

Even though the tabernacle was set up, seven of the twelve tribes had still not received their land. Moving the camp from Gilgal to Shiloh and resting after the major battles had paused the division of the country. The seven remaining tribes were left waiting without knowing exactly where their homes would be.

Joshua challenged the Israelites for putting off the work of claiming their territory. The people had grown comfortable living off the spoils of war and hesitated to take on the effort of clearing and settling new land. Joshua warned them that delay would only give their enemies time to regain strength.

Joshua told the seven unsettled tribes to choose three men from each tribe, making twenty-one men in total. He commissioned them to walk through the remaining regions and write down a description of the land and its towns. This careful survey would provide fair facts so no tribe would feel cheated.

The surveyors were ordered to divide the remaining country into seven equal parts. Judah was to keep its established borders in the south, and the tribes of Joseph would stay in their territory to the north. Those two large areas were already settled and were not to be disturbed.

After the surveyors wrote down their descriptions of the seven portions, they were to bring their report back to Joshua. He planned to cast lots before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle. Casting lots in God's presence meant God was the true judge of the division, helping everyone accept their home with gratitude.

Joshua reminded the people why only seven shares were needed. The Levites did not get a large territory because serving God as priests and receiving the holy offerings was their special inheritance. In addition, Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh had already received their land east of the Jordan River from Moses.

As the surveyors prepared to set out, Joshua repeated his instructions to go and explore the land thoroughly. He told them to write down what they found and return to the camp at Shiloh. There Joshua would cast lots before the Lord to distribute the land according to God's will.

The twenty-one men traveled through the country and wrote down a record of the towns, dividing the land into seven portions in a book. God kept them safe even while passing through areas where Canaanites still lived. When the survey was complete, they returned safely to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh.

Joshua cast the lots before the Lord at the tabernacle in Shiloh. Through this sacred act, he handed out the seven portions to the remaining tribes of Israel. Every tribe received its territory directly from God's hand.

The first lot drawn came up for the tribe of Benjamin. God's providence placed Benjamin's borders right between the strong tribes of Judah on the south and Joseph on the north. This fulfilled Moses' ancient blessing that Benjamin would dwell safely between the shoulders of his brothers under the Lord's protection.

These verses map out Benjamin's northern and western boundaries. The northern line started at the Jordan River, climbed past Jericho into the hill country, and passed south of Bethel down toward Lower Beth-horon. From the hill near Beth-horon, the western border turned southward until it ended at Kiriath-jearim on Judah's border.

Benjamin's southern border began near Kiriath-jearim and ran eastward past the spring at the Waters of Nephtoah. It then went down into the Valley of Hinnom, running along the southern slope of the Jebusite stronghold of Jerusalem toward En-rogel. This boundary formed the shared border with the tribe of Judah.

The southern boundary continued eastward past En-shemesh and Geliloth to the Stone of Bohan. From there it went down into the Jordan valley and passed Beth-hoglah. The southern border ended at the northern bay where the Jordan River empties into the Salt Sea, which is the Dead Sea.

The eastern border of Benjamin was formed by the Jordan River. These lines clearly marked out all four sides of the land given to the clans of Benjamin. God had carefully set the boundaries of their home.

The first list of Benjamin's cities names Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel. Although the walls of Jericho had been destroyed, the surrounding area still belonged to Benjamin. Bethel was a famous historical site on Benjamin's northern border where Jacob had seen his vision of God.

Six more eastern towns are listed: Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba, making twelve cities in all along with their villages. Geba was a notable hill town that later served as an important priestly center and military outpost.

These verses name nine more towns located mainly in the central and western hill country of Benjamin. This group included Gibeon, Ramah, and Mizpeh, which became famous in Israel's history as central gathering places for prayer and national decisions.

The final group contains fourteen towns, including Zelah, Gibeah, and Jebus, which is Jerusalem. Although Jerusalem lay within Benjamin's boundary line, it sat directly on the border with Judah and remained a Jebusite stronghold until King David captured it centuries later. This complete list marked the inheritance granted to the families of Benjamin.
